\chapter{-ario --- the Eighth and Last Ending}
\label{ch:ario}
\hlchaptermodality{63}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read an -ario word as English -ary and tell noun from adjective.}

I can read an -ario word as English -ary and tell noun from adjective.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[-ario]{-ario}

\label{lesson:ES-C09-ario}



\begin{quote}
\emph{-ncia}? (\emph{\textbf{-nce}}.) \emph{-oso}? (\emph{\textbf{-ous}}.)

One more, and the set is complete.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: belonging to, or the place for}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Spanish \emph{-ario} is English \emph{-ary}.}
\end{quote}

Latin \textbf{-ārius} meant \emph{belonging to} — and then, by an easy step, \emph{the place where that thing is kept}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{diccionario} — the place the \textbf{words} are kept
\end{quote}

Which is exactly what an English \textbf{dictionary} is, and neither language ever said so out loud.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{necesario} & \textbf{necessary} \\
\emph{ordinario} & \textbf{ordinary} \\
\emph{primario} & \textbf{primary} \\
\emph{diccionario} & \textbf{dictionary} \\
\emph{aniversario} & \textbf{anniversary} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: it does two jobs}]
Unlike the other seven, \emph{-ario} makes \textbf{both} nouns and adjectives, and the sentence tells you which:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{un diccionario} & a dictionary — a \textbf{thing} \\
\emph{es necesario} & it is necessary — a \textbf{quality} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

When it is an adjective it ends in \emph{-o}, so it shifts the way you already expect: \emph{necesario} / \emph{necesaria}. When it is a noun it is masculine, and takes \emph{el} or \emph{un}.

You do not have to decide in advance. The sentence decides.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{necesario, ordinario, primario}
  \item \emph{un diccionario}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{-ario} in English? (\emph{\textbf{-ary}}.) Noun or adjective? (\textbf{Either} — the sentence decides.)
\end{tcolorbox}
